text: Orina, along with her variants, is the primary female character in the novel. In a sense, she is the only female figure in *Between Dog and Wolf*. As D.B. Johnson summarizes, the “promiscuous heroine Orina-Mariia is a train dispatcher, a princess in her dispatcher’s tower, who entertains her coworkers in her bed. Some of her orgiastic trysts take place near the train tracks to which her lovers tie her meddling husband Il'ia. Orina, in at least one time dimension, is killed by a train as she belatedly tries to save Il'ia who loses his leg” (“Twilight Cosmos” 647). Ilya is obsessed with this woman, and this passion “is the ultimate source of the woes that befall Il'ia, the itinerant grinder. It is his passion for the faithless slut Orina that brings about his misfortunes: the loss of his leg, his wandering life as a drunken grinder, and the grisly events that lead to his death” (643). Orina, alternatively called Maria, exists in the book also in another version, as *ta dama*, that dame, “a mysterious woman who appears along the river seeking Il'ia and, failing to find him, takes away a new lover each time [...]. Her chance lovers return days later, sexually depleted and without interest in life. They usually die by their own hand” (645). In this figure (which embodies “virtually all female figures in the book,” D.B. Johnson, “Sasha Sokolov’s *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 211), Sokolov merges two of his major literary themes: sex and death. Thus, Orina, Maria, that dame (*ta dama*, *ta devochka*, *ta bobylka*, *ta babulya* — all linked by the demonstrative “ta”), “Life Everlastin,” and death in general make up a unique polymorphic character. Smith notices that this female figure “does not appear at all in the verse. The episode of the sexual encounter between this figure and the sailors, which reoccurs obsessively in the prose, is correspondingly absent from the verse passages” (333). Olga Matich suggests the existence of a literary subtext for Sokolov’s novel: “Pilniak’s lesser known story *Mother Earth* (*Mat' syra zemlia* 1927) about the violent confrontation between a naive young Bolshevik and an archaic Volga peasant community at the time of the Civil War. It is a kind of love story between the city-bred Bolshevik and the horse-tanner and young earth mother Arina, impaled by the Cossacks in one of the story’s many violence-ridden episodes. A variation on the Scythian juxtaposition of nature and culture, the story also depicts Arina’s maternal love for a fox cub, whom she tries to tame, thinking it is a wolf” (“Sasha Sokolov and His Literary Context” 312). The name Orina may also carry an echo of Pushkin's famous nurse Arina Rodionovna (Toker 353). Mario Caramitti proposes three recurring hypostases of ta dama across Sokolov’s novels: a first hypostasis is that of a “mysterious woman carrying an obscure menace and/or sexual temptation”; a second hypostasis is that of an “apparently better defined and concrete woman being the object of desire for the main character”; and the third hypostasis is that of a “child-woman, often mentally retarded, often victim of violences, who touches upon a slightly more sublimated erotic sphere” (“Amore e morte” 114). Caramitti also adds that in the novel one of *ta dama*'s victims, before or after committing suicide, explicitly calls her “вечная жизнь” (Life Everlastin): “it is precisely in the coitus with eternity, in a region of oblivion that it is most difficult to place on this side or on the other side of the Lethe, that the male protagonist finds the widest surface of contact with this protean female entity of now vast symbolic implications” (118). Among Orina’s many lovers and among the men who take advantage of her, there is also Yakov, her son, who is in a way “re-enacting the role of the lame Oedipus” (Johnson, “Sasha Sokolov’s *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 212). In chapter 14, Orina’s patronymic is said to be “Ignat’evna” (daughter of Ignatii): the name Ignatii possibly comes from the Latin "ignis" (fire) (R258/E190). Given that Orina is depicted here through her lust, such a patronymic seems apt. Her last name is said to be alternatively Neklina and Paklina (Spacklin, in translation): “You were called around the barracks Orina Neklina, and to whom do you belong now, to what kind of, let’s suppose, Spacklin, ah?” (R246/E169). The terms паклен and неклен are named for the Tatar maple (note the slight differences in the spelling between the tree names and Orina’s surnames: Неклина, Паклина). As Sokolov explains,  “Apparently, the author of the Notes and Ilya know or have heard about a man named Paklin. Ilya says that Arina's last name was Neklina, probably after one of her men. This episode is already briefly alluded to in chapter 1: “He was the one that adored scrapin and rollin over the slick on his sharps, which additionally resulted in us losin a client, and the undertakers, in contrast, findin one” (R150/E3).

text: Nikolay Ugodnik (Helperov in Boguslawski’s translation) is sometimes addressed with the diminutive Nikolka/Kolya. He is the protagonist of Note XVIII, “Transfiguration of Nikolay Helperov.” Here he is described in this manner: “We are pilgrims—he’s one far above us all, / We are cripples—he’s one far above the rest.” At the end of the Note, after a night of heavy drinking, Nikolay is transfigured (he has died): “Kolya learned to fly! / Crutches—like a pair of wings he bore. / He had turned into a falcon, poor old guy. / Drank too much. And he simply was no more.” (R204–205/E96). His life as “sincere loser in this world” is actually told by Ilya in chapter 1: his wife “got together with a wolf slayer and chased the Helper away from the house”; then, he tried to find a place to stay in Gorodnishche but was refused refuge at the “shelter for the unhearin”; he finally finds a place at the “house of the transient homeless,” but soon the “dame” notices him and asks: “Who’s the one so unsightly over there among you at the rink? Not to worry; it’s just Nikolka here among us skatin at the rink.” She asks the almshouse’s tenants to not let him live there forever, and after he leaves the house, it is reported that “durin a drunken incident got slightly upset and vanished somewhere, and it’s rather unlikely he’ll return” (R1501–151/E3–4). However, there is a second Nikolay in the book (appearing already in chapter 1), a young man from the village of Ploski (thus he is also called “Nikolay Ploskovsky”) who “never had his own name or, more precisely, had, but too long ago. And when that Nikolay the Helper went thru his transfiguration and flew away, this one snatched his name for himself—he did not allow, as they say, the goods to get wasted” (R153/E8). The name Nikolay (Nicholas) comes from the Greek words for “victory” and “people.” According to Eastern Orthodoxy, Nikolay Ugodnik (or Nikolay Chudotvorets, the Wonderworker) is Saint Nicholas, bishop of Myra (also known as Saint Nicholas of Bari), patron saint of travelers (sailors, merchants), prisoners, orphans and children in general, and others. Saint Nicholas is profoundly venerated by Russian Orthodoxy, and his life is often interpreted as concretizing various key ideas (wandering or continuous motion as source of salvation and purity; a mix of “otherness” and belonging). The figure of Saint Nicholas has served as the basis for a number of folkloric legends in Eastern Slavic tradition, and one of the most popular tales describes Nicholas as a wanderer across the Russian lands testing people for generosity, piety, and hospitality (see also T. Tsivian’s article “Nikolai Ugodnik — strannik na Russkoi zemle” 59).

text: A shoe with a slight heel, boot, and curved toe. Yakov mentions in Note 2 that the "lonesome babe" chides him for abandoning his boots (R165/E29). D.B. Johnson has identified more than twenty different types of shoes across Sokolov’s three novels: “*bashmaki, botforty, boty, botinki (polubotinki), cheboty, chizmy, chubury, galoshi (kaloshi), gety, ichigi, kedy, klogi, lapti, mokrostupy, obuvi (obuvki), sapogi, sandalii, tapochki (polutapochki), shlepantsy, shtiblety, tapti, tufli, valenki*. The list may easily be extended with appurtenances such as socks, stockings, footcloths, gaiters, skates, crutches, and artificial legs” (“The Galoshes Manifesto” 156). Regarding *Between Dog and Wolf*, he notes that Ilya’s last name immediately evokes Cinderella’s vair slippers. Johnson observes that “the footwear motif is Sokolov’s tribute, both conscious and unconscious, to the tradition in Russian literature represented by his predecessors – Ivan Bunin and Valentin Kataev” (179). In an interview with A. and N. Voronel', Sokolov calls Bunin, along with Gogol, his "contemporaries, collaborators along a chain, older masters" (Voroneli, "Ia khochu" 184). Shoe motif.

text: Nikolai is, apparently, blind, deaf, and mute. Caramitti talks about an "infinite gallery of crippled" (бесконечная галерея калек) in Sokolov's oeuvre ("Mul'tfil'm" 363). Two of Sokolov's early stories were about the blind as well: "The Old Helmsman" ("Staryi shturman") and "All the Colors of the Rainbow" ("Vse tsveta radugi"). Elena Kravchenko notes a parallel between this theme in Sokolov's first published stories and the nature of his writing in general: "They were published in Braille, the language by which corporality took the centre stage, outlasting the artefact of reality: not its expression but its embodiment" (*The Prose* 2).

text: The stress should fall on the last syllable. In ancient Russia, a *sloboda* referred to a settlement found in Povolzhye, Central Russia, Belarus, or Ukraine. The term is derived from the word for freedom. These tax-free settlements came to an end in the early eighteenth century when the practice was abolished and the settlements became regular villages. Often these suburbs were eventually subsumed by nearby cities. Today, *sloboda* refers to a rural locality in various oblasts. Sokolov attests that a [Sloboda](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Sloboda,+Tver+Oblast,+Russia,+171265/@56.6543229,36.4671174,12.92z/data=!4m6!3m5!1s0x46b4337b61338bc3:0xfd78ee1285635920!8m2!3d56.6502347!4d36.4718922!16s%2Fg%2F12xpjjzgs?entry=ttu) can be found by the [Volga River](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Volga+River/@51.9460656,41.3847096,5z/data=!3m1!4b1!4m6!3m5!1s0x41abfea34a299a3b:0x82d872a65cbe9fbb!8m2!3d51.3087451!4d45.7974619!16zL20vMGgyaHc?entry=ttu) in Konakovskii raion (personal communication, June 7, 2023).

Подобные поселения, свободные от повинностей, были упразднены в начале XVIII века и стали обыкновенными деревнями. Зачастую, пригородные районы поглощались близлежащими городами. В современном языке, "слобода" в разных областях относится к населенному пункту в сельской местности. Соколов подтверждет, что [Слобода](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Sloboda,+Tver+Oblast,+Russia,+171265/@56.6543229,36.4671174,12.92z/data=!4m6!3m5!1s0x46b4337b61338bc3:0xfd78ee1285635920!8m2!3d56.6502347!4d36.4718922!16s%2Fg%2F12xpjjzgs?entry=ttu) может быть найдена у [реки Волга](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Volga+River/@51.9460656,41.3847096,5z/data=!3m1!4b1!4m6!3m5!1s0x41abfea34a299a3b:0x82d872a65cbe9fbb!8m2!3d51.3087451!4d45.7974619!16zL20vMGgyaHc?entry=ttu) в Конаковском районе (личная переписка, 7 июня 2023).

text: Krylobyl is a key character dwelling in the world of the dead (living on the other shore of the Itil' river). It is not surprising given his "speaking name" formed by the words "krylo" (wing) and "byl" (was, used to be). He is a hypostasis of an angelic creature guiding Ilya in his wanderings and suggesting to him ideas and reflections: in chapter 4 it will be Krylobyl who advances the idea of the origin of the "zhe" letter; it is Krylobyl in the fourteenth chapter whom Ilya describes as a "know-it-all" who "instructs," the one "whom I trust, whom I praise" (R261/E197). In a sense, Krylobyl is Ilya's Virgil or, even, Beatrice in his wandering across this very special Inferno, Purgatorio, and Paradiso. Toward the end of the novel, he will be addressed by the narrator in chapter 16 (R275/E220) and by Ilya in chapter 17 as "Fedot Fyodorov" (R279/E227).

text: Ilya is *Between Dog and Wolf*’s protagonist and the author of what he calls the *Zaitil'shchina*, a long letter with epic traits (starting from its title) addressed to Inspector Pozhilykh in which he comments on the theft of his crutches (he has only one leg) and, more generally, describes life along the [Volga River](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Volga+River,+Russia/data=!4m2!3m1!1s0x41abfea34a299a3b:0x82d872a65cbe9fbb?sa=X&ved=2ahUKEwjCze_A-uj_AhVzrYkEHbRJBJkQ8gF6BAhoEAA&ved=2ahUKEwjCze_A-uj_AhVzrYkEHbRJBJkQ8gF6BQiEARAB). Johnson defines Ilya’s letter as “semiliterate ramblings,” aptly suggesting the style and register the reader will encounter in the novel (“*Sokolov’s Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 212). However, this character expresses at the same time a highly poetic and imaginative gaze. Ilya frequently associates himself with the biblical prophet Elijah, a figure folklorically linked with thunderstorms and which in Slavic tradition acquired some of the characteristics of the pagan God of the sky and thunder, Perun. Ilya is closely related to other key characters of the novel: he describes his troubled relationship with Orina (alternatively called Maria and the Dame) with whom he has a son; in encountering Yakov (the focus of several chapters), he suggests the possibility of being his father. The Oedipal plot resulting from this triangle has been noted by scholars, such as Johnson, who writes that “the game warden Iakov lusts for his mother (reincarnate as a mentally defective girl) and kills his father-all without being aware of the identity of either” (“Twilight Cosmos” 644).
ru_trans: Илья — главный герой "Между собакой и волком" и автор того, что он называет "Заитильщиной" — длинного эпического письма (начиная с названия), адресованного инспектору Пожилых, в котором он комментирует кражу своих костылей (у него лишь одна нога) и, в более общем плане, описывает жизнь на Приволжье. Джонсон определяет письмо Ильи как "полуграмотный бред", удачно указывая на стиль и тон, с которыми читатель встретится в романе (Johnson, "Sokolov’s *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition" 212). Однако данный персонаж выражает в то же время весьма поэтический и образный взгляд. Илья часто сравнивает себя с библейским пророком Илией — фольклорно связанной с грозой фигурой, которая в славянской традиции приобрела некоторые черты языческого бога неба и грома Перуна. Илья тесно связан с другими ключевыми персонажами романа: он описывает свои непростые отношения с Ориной (также известной нам как Мария и Дама), от которой у него есть сын; при встрече с Яковом (центральным персонажем нескольких глав) Илья начинает подозревает, что может быть его отцом. Эдипов сюжет, связывающий этот треугольник персонажей, был отмечен разными экспертами, например, Джонсоном, который пишет, что "егерь Яков испытывает физическое влечение к своей матери (перевоплощенной в умственно отсталую девушку) и убивает своего отца — все это не зная истинной сущности обоих" ("Twilight Cosmos" 644).

text: An unusual surname that does not permit standard declination. It literally means Elderly. Ostanin suggests a connection to Boris Pasternak's novel *Doctor Zhivago* by means of the root "zhiv" (to live) (10). Read the original [here](http://www.vehi.net/pasternak/). Likewise, he notes that Alexander Pushkin considered including a story entitled "Notes of an Elderly Person" in his cycle of short stories, *The Tales of Belkin*. Read the original [here](https://ilibrary.ru/text/89/index.html) and an English translation [here](https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/55219/pg55219-images.html). As Martina Napolitano observes, “Pozhilykh, Ilya’s addressee, is once ‘transfigured’ into an alleged Resurrection painting whose title plays on the ambiguity of his last name – *Voskresenie Pozhilykh*, *The Resurrection of the Elderly*. Ilya indeed concludes his letter wishing Pozhilykh “a happy resurrection”: this is his final message, his “good news.” It literally is his Gospel, from the Greek εὐαγγέλιον (*good news*);  in the original, Ilya here distorts the canonical *blagaia vest’* in ‘blagoe izvestie’” (“Studyin” 286).

text: A shoe with a slight heel, boot, and curved toe. Yakov mentions in Note 2 that the "lonesome babe" chides him for abandoning his boots (R165/E29). D.B. Johnson has identified more than twenty different types of shoes across Sokolov’s three novels: “*bashmaki, botforty, boty, botinki (polubotinki), cheboty, chizmy, chubury, galoshi (kaloshi), gety, ichigi, kedy, klogi, lapti, mokrostupy, obuvi (obuvki), sapogi, sandalii, tapochki (polutapochki), shlepantsy, shtiblety, tapti, tufli, valenki*. The list may easily be extended with appurtenances such as socks, stockings, footcloths, gaiters, skates, crutches, and artificial legs” (“The Galoshes Manifesto” 156). Regarding *Between Dog and Wolf*, he notes that Ilya’s last name immediately evokes Cinderella’s vair slippers. Johnson observes that “the footwear motif is Sokolov’s tribute, both conscious and unconscious, to the tradition in Russian literature represented by his predecessors – Ivan Bunin and Valentin Kataev” (179). In an interview with A. and N. Voronel', Sokolov calls Bunin, along with Gogol, his "contemporaries, collaborators along a chain, older masters" (Voroneli, "Ia khochu" 184). Shoe motif.

Однако данный персонаж выражает в то же время весьма поэтический и образный взгляд. Илья часто сравнивает себя с библейским пророком Илией — фольклорно связанной с грозой фигурой, которая в славянской традиции приобрела некоторые черты языческого бога неба и грома Перуна. Илья тесно связан с другими ключевыми персонажами романа: он описывает свои непростые отношения с Ориной (также известной нам как Мария и Дама), от которой у него есть сын; при встрече с Яковом (центральным персонажем нескольких глав) Илья начинает подозревает, что может быть его отцом. Эдипов сюжет, связывающий этот треугольник персонажей, был отмечен разными экспертами, например, Джонсоном, который пишет, что "егерь Яков испытывает физическое влечение к своей матери (перевоплощенной в умственно отсталую девушку) и убивает своего отца — все это не зная истинной сущности обоих" ("Twilight Cosmos" 644).

text: Ilya is *Between Dog and Wolf*’s protagonist and the author of what he calls the *Zaitil'shchina*, a long letter with epic traits (starting from its title) addressed to Inspector Pozhilykh in which he comments on the theft of his crutches (he has only one leg) and, more generally, describes life along the [Volga River](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Volga+River,+Russia/data=!4m2!3m1!1s0x41abfea34a299a3b:0x82d872a65cbe9fbb?sa=X&ved=2ahUKEwjCze_A-uj_AhVzrYkEHbRJBJkQ8gF6BAhoEAA&ved=2ahUKEwjCze_A-uj_AhVzrYkEHbRJBJkQ8gF6BQiEARAB). Johnson defines Ilya’s letter as “semiliterate ramblings,” aptly suggesting the style and register the reader will encounter in the novel (“*Sokolov’s Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 212). However, this character expresses at the same time a highly poetic and imaginative gaze. Ilya frequently associates himself with the biblical prophet Elijah, a figure folklorically linked with thunderstorms and which in Slavic tradition acquired some of the characteristics of the pagan God of the sky and thunder, Perun. Ilya is closely related to other key characters of the novel: he describes his troubled relationship with Orina (alternatively called Maria and the Dame) with whom he has a son; in encountering Yakov (the focus of several chapters), he suggests the possibility of being his father. The Oedipal plot resulting from this triangle has been noted by scholars, such as Johnson, who writes that “the game warden Iakov lusts for his mother (reincarnate as a mentally defective girl) and kills his father-all without being aware of the identity of either” (“Twilight Cosmos” 644).

text: In ancient Russia, a *sloboda* referred to a settlement found in Povolzhye, Central Russia, Belarus, or Ukraine. The term is derived from the word for freedom. These tax-free settlements came to an end in the early eighteenth century when the practice was abolished and the settlements became regular villages. Often these suburbs were eventually subsumed by nearby cities. Today, *sloboda* refers to a rural locality in various oblasts. Sokolov attests that a [Sloboda](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Sloboda,+Tver+Oblast,+Russia,+171265/@56.6543229,36.4671174,12.92z/data=!4m6!3m5!1s0x46b4337b61338bc3:0xfd78ee1285635920!8m2!3d56.6502347!4d36.4718922!16s%2Fg%2F12xpjjzgs?entry=ttu) can be found by the [Volga River](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Volga+River/@51.9460656,41.3847096,5z/data=!3m1!4b1!4m6!3m5!1s0x41abfea34a299a3b:0x82d872a65cbe9fbb!8m2!3d51.3087451!4d45.7974619!16zL20vMGgyaHc?entry=ttu) in Konakovskii raion (personal communication, June 7, 2023).

text: Ilya is *Between Dog and Wolf*’s protagonist and the author of what he calls the *Zaitil'shchina*, a long letter with epic traits (starting from its title) addressed to Inspector Pozhilykh in which he comments on the theft of his crutches (he has only one leg) and, more generally, describes life along the [Volga River](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Volga+River,+Russia/data=!4m2!3m1!1s0x41abfea34a299a3b:0x82d872a65cbe9fbb?sa=X&ved=2ahUKEwjCze_A-uj_AhVzrYkEHbRJBJkQ8gF6BAhoEAA&ved=2ahUKEwjCze_A-uj_AhVzrYkEHbRJBJkQ8gF6BQiEARAB). Johnson defines Ilya’s letter as “semiliterate ramblings,” aptly suggesting the style and register the reader will encounter in the novel (“*Sokolov’s Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 212). However, this character expresses at the same time a highly poetic and imaginative gaze. Ilya frequently associates himself with the biblical prophet Elijah, a figure folklorically linked with thunderstorms and which in Slavic tradition acquired some of the characteristics of the pagan God of the sky and thunder, Perun. Ilya is closely related to other key characters of the novel: he describes his troubled relationship with Orina (alternatively called Maria and the Dame) with whom he has a son; in encountering Yakov (the focus of several chapters), he suggests the possibility of being his father. The Oedipal plot resulting from this triangle has been noted by scholars, such as Johnson, who writes that “the game warden Iakov lusts for his mother (reincarnate as a mentally defective girl) and kills his father-all without being aware of the identity of either” (“Twilight Cosmos” 644).

text: An unusual surname that does not permit standard declination. It literally means Elderly. Ostanin suggests a connection to Boris Pasternak's novel *Doctor Zhivago* by means of the root "zhiv" (to live) (10). Read the original [here](http://www.vehi.net/pasternak/). Likewise, he notes that Alexander Pushkin considered including a story entitled "Notes of an Elderly Person" in his cycle of short stories, *The Tales of Belkin*. Read the original [here](https://ilibrary.ru/text/89/index.html) and an English translation [here](https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/55219/pg55219-images.html). As Martina Napolitano observes, “Pozhilykh, Ilya’s addressee, is once ‘transfigured’ into an alleged Resurrection painting whose title plays on the ambiguity of his last name – *Voskresenie Pozhilykh*, *The Resurrection of the Elderly*. Ilya indeed concludes his letter wishing Pozhilykh “a happy resurrection”: this is his final message, his “good news.” It literally is his Gospel, from the Greek εὐαγγέλιον (*good news*);  in the original, Ilya here distorts the canonical *blagaia vest’* in ‘blagoe izvestie’” (“Studyin” 286).

text: Sokolov explains: "This is an ordinary village well with a windlass. The bucket is lowered and lifted with the aid of a windlass and a rope wrapped around it. From time to time in some village someone falls into the well wanting to draw water. Sometimes a child, sometimes a drunken adult. Sometimes a dog or a cat. If there is water in the well, the victim drowns. But if the well is dry, there is a chance that sooner or later the person or animal will be pulled out. They will if people hear screams or meows for help. It is impossible to get out of the well by yourself. The huntsman Ilya tells us about most likely fell into the well, as they say, because he was drunk, and his wife hastened to take advantage of this circumstance. There is nothing allegorical in the fall of the huntsman into the well" (personal communication, June 7, 2023).
ru_trans: Соколов объясняет: "Имеется в виду обычный деревенский колодец с воротом. С помощью ворота и намотанной на него веревки осуществляют спуск и подъем ведра. Время от времени то в той деревне, то в этой кто-нибудь, желая зачерпнуть воды, падает в колодец. Иногда ребенок, иногда пьяный взрослый. Подчас собака или кошка. Если в колодце есть вода, жертва тонет. А если колодец сухой, то есть шанс, что рано или поздно человека или животное вытащат оттуда. Вытащат, если услышат крики или мяуканья о помощи. text: A Nikolai different from Nikolai the Helper, introduced above. Nikolay Ugodnik (Helperov in Boguslawski’s translation) is sometimes addressed with the diminutive Kolya. He is the protagonist of Note XVIII, “Transfiguration of Nikolay Helperov.” Here he is described in this manner: “We are pilgrims—he’s one far above us all, / We are cripples—he’s one far above the rest.” At the end of the Note, after a night of heavy drinking, Nikolay is transfigured (he has died): “Kolya learned to fly! / Crutches—like a pair of wings he bore. / He had turned into a falcon, poor old guy. / Drank too much. And he simply was no more.” (R204–205/E96). His life as “sincere loser in this world” is actually told by Ilya in chapter 1: his wife “got together with a wolf slayer and chased the Helper away from the house”; then, he tried to find a place to stay in Gorodnishche but was refused refuge at the “shelter for the unhearin”; he finally finds a place at the “house of the transient homeless,” but soon the “dame” notices him and asks: “Who’s the one so unsightly over there among you at the rink? Not to worry; it’s just Nikolka here among us skatin at the rink.” She asks the almshouse’s tenants to not let him live there forever, and after he leaves the house, it is reported that “durin a drunken incident got slightly upset and vanished somewhere, and it’s rather unlikely he’ll return” (R1501–151/E3–4). However, there is a second Nikolay in the book (appearing already in chapter 1), a young man from the village of Ploski (thus he is also called “Nikolay Ploskovsky”) who “never had his own name or, more precisely, had, but too long ago. And when that Nikolay the Helper went thru his transfiguration and flew away, this one snatched his name for himself—he did not allow, as they say, the goods to get wasted” (R153/E8). The name Nikolay (Nicholas) comes from the Greek words for “victory” and “people.” According to Eastern Orthodoxy, Nikolay Ugodnik (or Nikolay Chudotvorets, the Wonderworker) is Saint Nicholas, bishop of Myra (also known as Saint Nicholas of Bari), patron saint of travelers (sailors, merchants), prisoners, orphans and children in general, and others. Saint Nicholas is profoundly venerated by Russian Orthodoxy, and his life is often interpreted as concretizing various key ideas (wandering or continuous motion as source of salvation and purity; a mix of “otherness” and belonging). The figure of Saint Nicholas has served as the basis for a number of folkloric legends in Eastern Slavic tradition, and one of the most popular tales describes Nicholas as a wanderer across the Russian lands testing people for generosity, piety, and hospitality (see also T. Tsivian’s article “Nikolai Ugodnik — strannik na Russkoi zemle” 59).
ru_trans: Другой Николай, не относящийся к Николаю Угоднику, описанному выше. Николай Угодник (сокращённо — Коля) — протагонист Записки 18, "Преображение Николая Угодникова". Там он описывается следующим образом: "Мы — калики, он — калика из калик, / Мы — калеки, он — калека средь калек." В конце Записки говорится, что после ночи тяжелого пьянства Николай преображается (умирает): "летит Коля-Николай: / Костыли — как два крыла над головой. / Обратился, бедолага, в сокола́: / Перепил. И боле не было его" (R204–205/E96). О жизни Николая как "выступавшего по́ миру искреннего незадачника" рассказывает Илья в главе 1: его жена "поладила с волкобоем и сжила Угодника долой со двора"; затем он пытается найти ночлег в Городнище и встречает отказ от "незрячего приюта", но наконец останавливается в "доме заезжих бездомных", "дама" замечает его и спрашивает: "Что это там у вас между вами невзрачный какой на катке? Не беспокойся, это просто Николка у нас между нами катается себе на катке." Она просит владельцев приюта, чтобы они не позволили ему задержаться навсегда. После того, как Николай покидает заведание, сообщается, что он "по пьяному делу маленько погорячился и куда-то такое пропал, да и вряд ли, пожалуй, объявится" (R1501–151/E3–4). Впрочем, в книге также есть и второй Николай, уже появлявшийся в главе 1: молодой человек из Плосков (поэтому его и зовут Николай Плосковский), "у которого имени собственного не было никогда, верней, было, но слишком давно. И когда Николаю Угоднику вышло преображение и он улетел, этот имя его себе урвал — не дал, называется, добру пропасть" (R153/E8). Имя Николай (Николас) происходит от греческих определений "победы" и "людей". Согласно восточному православию, Николай Угодник (Николай Чудотворец, Святитель Николай) — Святой Николас, архиепископ Мир Ликийских (также известен как Святой Николай Барийский), святой покровитель путешественников (моряков, торговцев), заключенных, сирот, детей в принципе и остальных. Николай Чудотворец глубоко почитается в русском православии, а его жизнь интерпретируется как воплощение ряда важнейших представлений (блуждание или непрерывное движение как источник спасения и очищения; сочетание "инаковости" и чувства связи, сопричастности). Его образ послужил фундаментом для различных фольклорных сюжетов в восточнославянской традиции. Одна из самых известных сказок рассказывает о Николае как о страннике, блуждающего по русским землям и проверяющего людей на щедрость, благочестие и гостеприимство (см. также T. Tsivian, article "Nikolai Ugodnik — strannik na Russkoi zemle" 59).

text: Death. The reference is to the biblical Transfiguration of Jesus, in which Jesus goes to a mountaintop to pray with James, John, and Mark. Once there, he begins to shine with light, and Elijah (one of Ilya's identities in the novel) and Moses appear beside him as the voice of God calls out to him. The event is documented in [Matthew 17:1–8](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Matthew%2017%3A1-8&version=NIV), [Mark 9:2–8](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Mark%209%3A2-8&version=NIV), and [Luke 9:28–36](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Luke%209%3A28-36&version=NIV). Celebrated on August 6. The main character of Mikhail Bulgakov's *Heart of a Dog* (a novel which widely circulated in samizdat in the 60s) is Doctor Preobrazhensky, whose experiment of turning a homeless dog into a man leads to tragic consequences (and to his "transfigurating" back into a dog). Locally, this concept and its relationship to death also figures prominently in Note XVIII (R204–205/E95–96).
ru_trans: Смерть. Отсылка к библейскому Преображению Иисуса, когда Иисус поднимается на гору с Иаковом, Иоанном и Марком. Там, на вершине, он начинает сиять, а рядом с ним появляются пророк Илия (одна из личностей Ильи в романе) и Моисей, в то время как к нему взывает Божий голос. Это событие описано в [Матфея 17:1-8](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Matthew+17%3A1-8&version=RUSV), [Марка 9:2-8](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Mark+9%3A2-8&version=RUSV), [Луки 9:28-36](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Luke+9%3A28-36&version=RUSV). Празднуется 6 августа. Кроме того, главный герой романа Михаила Булгакова "Сердце собаки" (одно из массовых произведений самиздата 60-ых) — доктор Преображенский, чей эксперимент по превращению бездомного пса в человека ведет к плачевному исходу (и его "преображению" обратно в собаку). Локально, концепция преображения и ее связь со смертью играет значительную роль в Записке XVIII (R204–205/E95–96).

text: Ilya is *Between Dog and Wolf*’s protagonist and the author of what he calls the *Zaitil'shchina*, a long letter with epic traits (starting from its title) addressed to Inspector Pozhilykh in which he comments on the theft of his crutches (he has only one leg) and, more generally, describes life along the [Volga River](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Volga+River,+Russia/data=!4m2!3m1!1s0x41abfea34a299a3b:0x82d872a65cbe9fbb?sa=X&ved=2ahUKEwjCze_A-uj_AhVzrYkEHbRJBJkQ8gF6BAhoEAA&ved=2ahUKEwjCze_A-uj_AhVzrYkEHbRJBJkQ8gF6BQiEARAB). Johnson defines Ilya’s letter as “semiliterate ramblings,” aptly suggesting the style and register the reader will encounter in the novel (“*Sokolov’s Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 212). However, this character expresses at the same time a highly poetic and imaginative gaze. Ilya frequently associates himself with the biblical prophet Elijah, a figure folklorically linked with thunderstorms and which in Slavic tradition acquired some of the characteristics of the pagan God of the sky and thunder, Perun. Ilya is closely related to other key characters of the novel: he describes his troubled relationship with Orina (alternatively called Maria and the Dame) with whom he has a son; in encountering Yakov (the focus of several chapters), he suggests the possibility of being his father. The Oedipal plot resulting from this triangle has been noted by scholars, such as Johnson, who writes that “the game warden Iakov lusts for his mother (reincarnate as a mentally defective girl) and kills his father-all without being aware of the identity of either” (“Twilight Cosmos” 644).

text: Gury is one of the hunters living by the river. His death is described in detail in chapter 14: during an ice race, “a few verstas before the turn, Gury began gainin and the whipper-in fallin behind, but Gury aimed slightly more to the right than he should and fell into a polynya, an ice hole in the area of the fairway. [...] he plopped in and right away got sucked under the ice.” Since his body cannot be found until spring, his funeral is organized “without his factual presence” (R260/E196). This episode is already briefly alluded to in chapter 1: “He was the one that adored scrapin and rollin over the slick on his sharps, which additionally resulted in us losin a client, and the undertakers, in contrast, findin one” (R150/E3).

text: In ancient Russia, a *sloboda* referred to a settlement found in Povolzhye, Central Russia, Belarus, or Ukraine. The term is derived from the word for freedom. These tax-free settlements came to an end in the early eighteenth century when the practice was abolished and the settlements became regular villages. Often these suburbs were eventually subsumed by nearby cities. Today, *sloboda* refers to a rural locality in various oblasts. Sokolov attests that a [Sloboda](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Sloboda,+Tver+Oblast,+Russia,+171265/@56.6543229,36.4671174,12.92z/data=!4m6!3m5!1s0x46b4337b61338bc3:0xfd78ee1285635920!8m2!3d56.6502347!4d36.4718922!16s%2Fg%2F12xpjjzgs?entry=ttu) can be found by the [Volga River](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Volga+River/@51.9460656,41.3847096,5z/data=!3m1!4b1!4m6!3m5!1s0x41abfea34a299a3b:0x82d872a65cbe9fbb!8m2!3d51.3087451!4d45.7974619!16zL20vMGgyaHc?entry=ttu) in Konakovskii raion (personal communication, June 7, 2023).

text: Nikolai's name shortens to Nikola. Nikolay Ugodnik (Helperov in Boguslawski’s translation) is sometimes addressed with the diminutive Nikolka/Kolya. He is the protagonist of Note XVIII, “Transfiguration of Nikolay Helperov.” Here he is described in this manner: “We are pilgrims—he’s one far above us all, / We are cripples—he’s one far above the rest.” At the end of the Note, after a night of heavy drinking, Nikolay is transfigured (he has died): “Kolya learned to fly! / Crutches—like a pair of wings he bore. / He had turned into a falcon, poor old guy. / Drank too much. And he simply was no more.” (R204–205/E96). His life as “sincere loser in this world” is actually told by Ilya in chapter 1: his wife “got together with a wolf slayer and chased the Helper away from the house”; then, he tried to find a place to stay in Gorodnishche but was refused refuge at the “shelter for the unhearin”; he finally finds a place at the “house of the transient homeless,” but soon the “dame” notices him and asks: “Who’s the one so unsightly over there among you at the rink? Not to worry; it’s just Nikolka here among us skatin at the rink.” She asks the almshouse’s tenants to not let him live there forever, and after he leaves the house, it is reported that “durin a drunken incident got slightly upset and vanished somewhere, and it’s rather unlikely he’ll return” (R1501–151/E3–4). However, there is a second Nikolay in the book (appearing already in chapter 1), a young man from the village of Ploski (thus he is also called “Nikolay Ploskovsky”) who “never had his own name or, more precisely, had, but too long ago. And when that Nikolay the Helper went thru his transfiguration and flew away, this one snatched his name for himself—he did not allow, as they say, the goods to get wasted” (R153/E8). The name Nikolay (Nicholas) comes from the Greek words for “victory” and “people.” According to Eastern Orthodoxy, Nikolay Ugodnik (or Nikolay Chudotvorets, the Wonderworker) is Saint Nicholas, bishop of Myra (also known as Saint Nicholas of Bari), patron saint of travelers (sailors, merchants), prisoners, orphans and children in general, and others. Saint Nicholas is profoundly venerated by Russian Orthodoxy, and his life is often interpreted as concretizing various key ideas (wandering or continuous motion as source of salvation and purity; a mix of “otherness” and belonging). The figure of Saint Nicholas has served as the basis for a number of folkloric legends in Eastern Slavic tradition, and one of the most popular tales describes Nicholas as a wanderer across the Russian lands testing people for generosity, piety, and hospitality (see also T. Tsivian’s article “Nikolai Ugodnik — strannik na Russkoi zemle” 59).

Tsivian, article "Nikolai Ugodnik — strannik na Russkoi zemle" 59).

text: Traditional Russian winter felt boots. The one-legged Ilya will be associated with the trapper who lives under the stairs and works with animal furs. D.B. Johnson has identified more than twenty different types of shoes across Sokolov’s three novels: “*bashmaki, botforty, boty, botinki (polubotinki), cheboty, chizmy, chubury, galoshi (kaloshi), gety, ichigi, kedy, klogi, lapti, mokrostupy, obuvi (obuvki), sapogi, sandalii, tapochki (polutapochki), shlepantsy, shtiblety, tapti, tufli, valenki*. The list may easily be extended with appurtenances such as socks, stockings, footcloths, gaiters, skates, crutches, and artificial legs” (“The Galoshes Manifesto” 156). Regarding *Between Dog and Wolf*, he notes that Ilya’s last name immediately evokes Cinderella’s vair slippers. Johnson observes that “the footwear motif is Sokolov’s tribute, both conscious and unconscious, to the tradition in Russian literature represented by his predecessors – Ivan Bunin and Valentin Kataev” (179). In an interview with A. and N. Voronel', Sokolov calls Bunin, along with Gogol, his "contemporaries, collaborators along a chain, older masters" (Voroneli, "Ia khochu" 184). Shoe motif.

text: Nikola --> Nikolay. Nikolay Ugodnik (Helperov in Boguslawski’s translation) is sometimes addressed with the diminutive Kolya. He is the protagonist of Note XVIII, “Transfiguration of Nikolay Helperov.” Here he is described in this manner: “We are pilgrims—he’s one far above us all, / We are cripples—he’s one far above the rest.” At the end of the Note, after a night of heavy drinking, Nikolay is transfigured (he has died): “Kolya learned to fly! / Crutches—like a pair of wings he bore. / He had turned into a falcon, poor old guy. / Drank too much. And he simply was no more.” (R204–205/E96). His life as “sincere loser in this world” is actually told by Ilya in chapter 1: his wife “got together with a wolf slayer and chased the Helper away from the house”; then, he tried to find a place to stay in Gorodnishche but was refused refuge at the “shelter for the unhearin”; he finally finds a place at the “house of the transient homeless,” but soon the “dame” notices him and asks: “Who’s the one so unsightly over there among you at the rink? Not to worry; it’s just Nikolka here among us skatin at the rink.” She asks the almshouse’s tenants to not let him live there forever, and after he leaves the house, it is reported that “durin a drunken incident got slightly upset and vanished somewhere, and it’s rather unlikely he’ll return” (R1501–151/E3–4). However, there is a second Nikolay in the book (appearing already in chapter 1), a young man from the village of Ploski (thus he is also called “Nikolay Ploskovsky”) who “never had his own name or, more precisely, had, but too long ago. And when that Nikolay the Helper went thru his transfiguration and flew away, this one snatched his name for himself—he did not allow, as they say, the goods to get wasted” (R153/E8). The name Nikolay (Nicholas) comes from the Greek words for “victory” and “people.” According to Eastern Orthodoxy, Nikolay Ugodnik (or Nikolay Chudotvorets, the Wonderworker) is Saint Nicholas, bishop of Myra (also known as Saint Nicholas of Bari), patron saint of travelers (sailors, merchants), prisoners, orphans and children in general, and others. Saint Nicholas is profoundly venerated by Russian Orthodoxy, and his life is often interpreted as concretizing various key ideas (wandering or continuous motion as source of salvation and purity; a mix of “otherness” and belonging). The figure of Saint Nicholas has served as the basis for a number of folkloric legends in Eastern Slavic tradition, and one of the most popular tales describes Nicholas as a wanderer across the Russian lands testing people for generosity, piety, and hospitality (see also T. Tsivian’s article “Nikolai Ugodnik — strannik na Russkoi zemle” 59).

text: The main setting of the novel: a fictional town on the banks of the Volga River. Also called Gorodnishchi. Derived from the words for town (gorod) and beggar (nishchii). It is the "town of beggars." Olga Matich writes: "If *School for Fools* was written against the background of youth prose, Sokolov's next novel *Between Dog and Wolf* may be read as the author's response to village prose, the literary rage of the seventies" ("Sasha Sokolov" 310). Vadim Kreid observes that Gorodnishche, a barracks village of beggars and thieves, resembles an "Anti-Kitezh" (Kitezh being the legendary, mythical city in Russian folklore that only the pure-hearted will have the chance to reach). In Gorodnishche, however, thieves rob beggars, while beggars beg thieves ("Zaitil'shchina" 213). According to Johnson, the living dwell Gorodnishche, while the dead reside on the other side of the river, in Bydogoshch ("Sokolov's *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition" 209). Johnson also mentions a statement by Sokolov himself: "Sokolov reports that the name is a blend of the dissolute eighteen-century town of Gorodnya described by A. N. Radishchev in his *Journey from Petersburg to Moscow* and a nearby town called Gorodishche. Thus the time layers of the sixteenth century, the eighteenth century, and a mythic present are all superimposed upon each other – a characteristic technique in the novel" (217).
ru_trans: Главное место действия романа: вымышленный город на берегу Волги; также называется Городнищи. Название получено в результате сочетания слов "город" и "нищий". Таким образом, Городнищи — город нищих. О. Матич пишет: "Если 'Школа для дураков' была написана в противовес молодежной прозе, следующий роман Соколова, 'Между собакой и волком' можно расценивать как ответ автора на деревенскую прозу, модное литературное направление семидесятых" (Matich "Sasha Sokolov" 310). В. Крейд замечает, что Городнище, барачный город нищих и воров, напоминает “Анти-Китеж” (Китеж — мифический город в русском фольклоре, в который попадают только чистые сердцем). В Городнище, однако, воры грабят нищих, и нищие попрошайничают у грабителей (Kreid "Zaitil'shchina" 213). Согласно Джонсону, Городнище — обитель живых, в то время как мертвые населяют противоположный берег реки, в Быдогощах (Johnson "Sokolov's ‘Between Dog and Wolf' and the Modernist Tradition’ 209). Джонсон также цитирует самого Соколова: “Соколов замечает, что название города является помесью развратного города XVIII века Городни, описанного А. Н. Радищевым в 'Путешествии из Петербурга в Москву' и близлежащего города Городище. Таким образом, временные слои XVI века, XVIII века и мифического настоящего накладываются друг на друга — типичный роману прием” (217).

Ostanin suggests a connection to Boris Pasternak's novel *Doctor Zhivago* by means of the root "zhiv" (to live) (10). Read the original [here](http://www.vehi.net/pasternak/). Likewise, he notes that Alexander Pushkin considered including a story entitled "Notes of an Elderly Person" in his cycle of short stories, *The Tales of Belkin*. Read the original [here](https://ilibrary.ru/text/89/index.html) and an English translation [here](https://www.gutenberg.org/cache/epub/55219/pg55219-images.html). As Martina Napolitano observes, “Pozhilykh, Ilya’s addressee, is once ‘transfigured’ into an alleged Resurrection painting whose title plays on the ambiguity of his last name – *Voskresenie Pozhilykh*, *The Resurrection of the Elderly*. Ilya indeed concludes his letter wishing Pozhilykh “a happy resurrection”: this is his final message, his “good news.” It literally is his Gospel, from the Greek εὐαγγέλιον (*good news*);  in the original, Ilya here distorts the canonical *blagaia vest’* in ‘blagoe izvestie’” (“Studyin” 286).

text: Gury is one of the hunters living by the river. His death is described in detail in chapter 14: during an ice race, “a few verstas before the turn, Gury began gainin and the whipper-in fallin behind, but Gury aimed slightly more to the right than he should and fell into a polynya, an ice hole in the area of the fairway. […] he plopped in and right away got sucked under the ice.” Since his body cannot be found until spring, his funeral is organized “without his factual presence” (R260/E196). This episode is already briefly alluded to in chapter 1: “He was the one that adored scrapin and rollin over the slick on his sharps, which additionally resulted in us losin a client, and the undertakers, in contrast, findin one” (R150/E3). The name is Jewish and means "little lion" (gur 'aryeh). There may be a connection to Titian's *Allegory of Prudence*. Ostanin suggests that it may be linked to Gury Kazansky (ca. 1500-1563) (14). text: Sokolov explains: "'plesnut' vzdrok' means to pour to the edge of the glass. text: A Nikolai different from Nikolay the Helper, introduced above. Nikolay Ugodnik (Helperov in Boguslawski’s translation) is sometimes addressed with the diminutive Kolya. And he simply was no more.” (R204–205/E96). His life as “sincere loser in this world” is actually told by Ilya in chapter 1: his wife “got together with a wolf slayer and chased the Helper away from the house”; then, he tried to find a place to stay in Gorodnishche but was refused refuge at the “shelter for the unhearin”; he finally finds a place at the “house of the transient homeless,” but soon the “dame” notices him and asks: “Who’s the one so unsightly over there among you at the rink? text: A Nikolai different from Nikolai the Helper, introduced above. Nikolay Ugodnik (Helperov in Boguslawski’s translation) is sometimes addressed with the diminutive Kolya. He is the protagonist of Note XVIII, “Transfiguration of Nikolay Helperov.” Here he is described in this manner: “We are pilgrims—he’s one far above us all, / We are cripples—he’s one far above the rest.” At the end of the Note, after a night of heavy drinking, Nikolay is transfigured (he has died): “Kolya learned to fly! / Crutches—like a pair of wings he bore. / He had turned into a falcon, poor old guy. / Drank too much. And he simply was no more.” (R204–205/E96). His life as “sincere loser in this world” is actually told by Ilya in chapter 1: his wife “got together with a wolf slayer and chased the Helper away from the house”; then, he tried to find a place to stay in Gorodnishche but was refused refuge at the “shelter for the unhearin”; he finally finds a place at the “house of the transient homeless,” but soon the “dame” notices him and asks: “Who’s the one so unsightly over there among you at the rink? Not to worry; it’s just Nikolka here among us skatin at the rink.” She asks the almshouse’s tenants to not let him live there forever, and after he leaves the house, it is reported that “durin a drunken incident got slightly upset and vanished somewhere, and it’s rather unlikely he’ll return” (R1501–151/E3–4). However, there is a second Nikolay in the book (appearing already in chapter 1), a young man from the village of Ploski (thus he is also called “Nikolay Ploskovsky”) who “never had his own name or, more precisely, had, but too long ago. And when that Nikolay the Helper went thru his transfiguration and flew away, this one snatched his name for himself—he did not allow, as they say, the goods to get wasted” (R153/E8). The name Nikolay (Nicholas) comes from the Greek words for “victory” and “people.” According to Eastern Orthodoxy, Nikolay Ugodnik (or Nikolay Chudotvorets, the Wonderworker) is Saint Nicholas, bishop of Myra (also known as Saint Nicholas of Bari), patron saint of travelers (sailors, merchants), prisoners, orphans and children in general, and others. Saint Nicholas is profoundly venerated by Russian Orthodoxy, and his life is often interpreted as concretizing various key ideas (wandering or continuous motion as source of salvation and purity; a mix of “otherness” and belonging). The figure of Saint Nicholas has served as the basis for a number of folkloric legends in Eastern Slavic tradition, and one of the most popular tales describes Nicholas as a wanderer across the Russian lands testing people for generosity, piety, and hospitality (see also T. Tsivian’s article “Nikolai Ugodnik — strannik na Russkoi zemle” 59).

text: Death. The reference is to the biblical Transfiguration of Jesus, in which Jesus goes to a mountaintop to pray with James, John, and Mark. Once there, he begins to shine with light, and Elijah (one of Ilya's identities in the novel) and Moses appear beside him as the voice of God calls out to him. The event is documented in [Matthew 17:1–8](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Matthew%2017%3A1-8&version=NIV), [Mark 9:2–8](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Mark%209%3A2-8&version=NIV), and [Luke 9:28–36](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Luke%209%3A28-36&version=NIV). Celebrated on August 6. The main character of Mikhail Bulgakov's *Heart of a Dog* (a novel which widely circulated in samizdat in the 60s) is Doctor Preobrazhensky, whose experiment of turning a homeless dog into a man leads to tragic consequences (and to his "transfigurating" back into a dog). Locally, this concept and its relationship to death also figures prominently in Note XVIII (R204–205/E95–96).

text: Gury is one of the hunters living by the river. His death is described in detail in chapter 14: during an ice race, “a few verstas before the turn, Gury began gainin and the whipper-in fallin behind, but Gury aimed slightly more to the right than he should and fell into a polynya, an ice hole in the area of the fairway. […] he plopped in and right away got sucked under the ice.” Since his body cannot be found until spring, his funeral is organized “without his factual presence” (R260/E196). This episode is already briefly alluded to in chapter 1: “He was the one that adored scrapin and rollin over the slick on his sharps, which additionally resulted in us losin a client, and the undertakers, in contrast, findin one” (R150/E3). The name is Jewish and means "little lion" (gur 'aryeh). There may be a connection to Titian's *Allegory of Prudence*. Ostanin suggests that it may be linked to Gury Kazansky (ca. 1500-1563) (14). ru_trans: Другой Николай, не относящийся к Николаю Угоднику, описанному выше. Николай Угодник (сокращённо — Коля) — протагонист Записки 18, "Преображение Николая Угодникова". Там он описывается следующим образом: "Мы — калики, он — калика из калик, / Мы — калеки, он — калека средь калек." В конце Записки говорится, что после ночи тяжелого пьянства Николай преображается (умирает): "летит Коля-Николай: / Костыли — как два крыла над головой. / Обратился, бедолага, в сокола́: / Перепил. И боле не было его" (R204–205/E96). О жизни Николая как "выступавшего по́ миру искреннего незадачника" рассказывает Илья в главе 1: его жена "поладила с волкобоем и сжила Угодника долой со двора"; затем он пытается найти ночлег в Городнище и встречает отказ от "незрячего приюта", но наконец останавливается в "доме заезжих бездомных", "дама" замечает его и спрашивает: "Что это там у вас между вами невзрачный какой на катке? Не беспокойся, это просто Николка у нас между нами катается себе на катке." Она просит владельцев приюта, чтобы они не позволили ему задержаться навсегда. После того, как Николай покидает заведание, сообщается, что он "по пьяному делу маленько погорячился и куда-то такое пропал, да и вряд ли, пожалуй, объявится" (R1501–151/E3–4). Впрочем, в книге также есть и второй Николай, уже появлявшийся в главе 1: молодой человек из Плосков (поэтому его и зовут Николай Плосковский), "у которого имени собственного не было никогда, верней, было, но слишком давно. И когда Николаю Угоднику вышло преображение и он улетел, этот имя его себе урвал — не дал, называется, добру пропасть" (R153/E8). Имя Николай (Николас) происходит от греческих определений "победы" и "людей". Согласно восточному православию, Николай Угодник (Николай Чудотворец, Святитель Николай) — Святой Николас, архиепископ Мир Ликийских (также известен как Святой Николай Барийский), святой покровитель путешественников (моряков, торговцев), заключенных, сирот, детей в принципе и остальных. Николай Чудотворец глубоко почитается в русском православии, а его жизнь интерпретируется как воплощение ряда важнейших представлений (блуждание или непрерывное движение как источник спасения и очищения; сочетание "инаковости" и чувства связи, сопричастности). Его образ послужил фундаментом для различных фольклорных сюжетов в восточнославянской традиции. Одна из самых известных сказок рассказывает о Николае как о страннике, блуждающего по русским землям и проверяющего людей на щедрость, благочестие и гостеприимство (см. также T. Tsivian, article "Nikolai Ugodnik — strannik na Russkoi zemle" 59).

text: A Nikolai different from Nikolay the Helper, introduced above. Nikolay Ugodnik (Helperov in Boguslawski’s translation) is sometimes addressed with the diminutive Kolya. He is the protagonist of Note XVIII, “Transfiguration of Nikolay Helperov.” Here he is described in this manner: “We are pilgrims—he’s one far above us all, / We are cripples—he’s one far above the rest.” At the end of the Note, after a night of heavy drinking, Nikolay is transfigured (he has died): “Kolya learned to fly! / Crutches—like a pair of wings he bore. / He had turned into a falcon, poor old guy. / Drank too much. And he simply was no more.” (R204–205/E96). His life as “sincere loser in this world” is actually told by Ilya in chapter 1: his wife “got together with a wolf slayer and chased the Helper away from the house”; then, he tried to find a place to stay in Gorodnishche but was refused refuge at the “shelter for the unhearin”; he finally finds a place at the “house of the transient homeless,” but soon the “dame” notices him and asks: “Who’s the one so unsightly over there among you at the rink? Not to worry; it’s just Nikolka here among us skatin at the rink.” She asks the almshouse’s tenants to not let him live there forever, and after he leaves the house, it is reported that “durin a drunken incident got slightly upset and vanished somewhere, and it’s rather unlikely he’ll return” (R1501–151/E3–4). However, there is a second Nikolay in the book (appearing already in chapter 1), a young man from the village of Ploski (thus he is also called “Nikolay Ploskovsky”) who “never had his own name or, more precisely, had, but too long ago. And when that Nikolay the Helper went thru his transfiguration and flew away, this one snatched his name for himself—he did not allow, as they say, the goods to get wasted” (R153/E8). The name Nikolay (Nicholas) comes from the Greek words for “victory” and “people.” According to Eastern Orthodoxy, Nikolay Ugodnik (or Nikolay Chudotvorets, the Wonderworker) is Saint Nicholas, bishop of Myra (also known as Saint Nicholas of Bari), patron saint of travelers (sailors, merchants), prisoners, orphans and children in general, and others. Saint Nicholas is profoundly venerated by Russian Orthodoxy, and his life is often interpreted as concretizing various key ideas (wandering or continuous motion as source of salvation and purity; a mix of “otherness” and belonging). The figure of Saint Nicholas has served as the basis for a number of folkloric legends in Eastern Slavic tradition, and one of the most popular tales describes Nicholas as a wanderer across the Russian lands testing people for generosity, piety, and hospitality (see also T. Tsivian’s article “Nikolai Ugodnik — strannik na Russkoi zemle” 59).

Tsivian, article "Nikolai Ugodnik — strannik na Russkoi zemle" 59).

text: Traditional Russian felt boots. The one-legged Ilya will be associated with the trapper who lives under the stairs and works with animal furs. D.B. Johnson has identified more than twenty different types of shoes across Sokolov’s three novels: “*bashmaki, botforty, boty, botinki (polubotinki), cheboty, chizmy, chubury, galoshi (kaloshi), gety, ichigi, kedy, klogi, lapti, mokrostupy, obuvi (obuvki), sapogi, sandalii, tapochki (polutapochki), shlepantsy, shtiblety, tapti, tufli, valenki*. The list may easily be extended with appurtenances such as socks, stockings, footcloths, gaiters, skates, crutches, and artificial legs” (“The Galoshes Manifesto” 156). Regarding *Between Dog and Wolf*, he notes that Ilya’s last name immediately evokes Cinderella’s vair slippers. Johnson observes that “the footwear motif is Sokolov’s tribute, both conscious and unconscious, to the tradition in Russian literature represented by his predecessors – Ivan Bunin and Valentin Kataev” (179). In an interview with A. and N. Voronel', Sokolov calls Bunin, along with Gogol, his "contemporaries, collaborators along a chain, older masters" (Voroneli, "Ia khochu" 184). Shoe motif.

text: Pyotr/Fyodor/Yegor. Pyotr, “one smart aleck from Sloboda” (R173/E43), is Pavel’s uncle and is sent by his nephew in Gorodnishche to find yeast (when the story is retold in chapter 14, it is the uncle asking Pavel to get yeast). He is alternatively called Fyodor and Yegor: the choice seems to be guided by the presence of the vowels "e/ë" and "o." The name Pyotr, from Greek, means “stone.” The apostle Peter (Simon Peter), in origin a fisherman, is considered the first Christian Pope. Peter denied Jesus three times during the events of the crucifixion, as Jesus had predicted (see [Matthew 26:69–75](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Matthew+26%3A69%E2%80%9375&version=NIV;NRT)). Fyodor (Theodore) means “God’s gift.” The name Egor is a variation of the name Georgy (George), from the Greek “farmer.” He was immortalized as a saint through the legend of the Dragon (Saint George the Dragon-slayer). In chapter 10 this character is challenged to hang himself, which results in his suicide.
ru_trans: Петр/Федор/Егор. Петр, "грамотей один слободский" (R173/E43), дядя Павла, которого племянник отправляет в Городнище за дрожжами (когда та же история пересказывается в главе 14, это дядя просит Павла добыть дрожжи). text: A Nikolai different from Nikolai the Helper, introduced above. Nikolay Ugodnik (Helperov in Boguslawski’s translation) is sometimes addressed with the diminutive Kolya. He is the protagonist of Note XVIII, “Transfiguration of Nikolay Helperov.” Here he is described in this manner: “We are pilgrims—he’s one far above us all, / We are cripples—he’s one far above the rest.” At the end of the Note, after a night of heavy drinking, Nikolay is transfigured (he has died): “Kolya learned to fly! / Crutches—like a pair of wings he bore. / He had turned into a falcon, poor old guy. / Drank too much. And he simply was no more.” (R204–205/E96). His life as “sincere loser in this world” is actually told by Ilya in chapter 1: his wife “got together with a wolf slayer and chased the Helper away from the house”; then, he tried to find a place to stay in Gorodnishche but was refused refuge at the “shelter for the unhearin”; he finally finds a place at the “house of the transient homeless,” but soon the “dame” notices him and asks: “Who’s the one so unsightly over there among you at the rink? Not to worry; it’s just Nikolka here among us skatin at the rink.” She asks the almshouse’s tenants to not let him live there forever, and after he leaves the house, it is reported that “durin a drunken incident got slightly upset and vanished somewhere, and it’s rather unlikely he’ll return” (R1501–151/E3–4). However, there is a second Nikolay in the book (appearing already in chapter 1), a young man from the village of Ploski (thus he is also called “Nikolay Ploskovsky”) who “never had his own name or, more precisely, had, but too long ago. And when that Nikolay the Helper went thru his transfiguration and flew away, this one snatched his name for himself—he did not allow, as they say, the goods to get wasted” (R153/E8). The name Nikolay (Nicholas) comes from the Greek words for “victory” and “people.” According to Eastern Orthodoxy, Nikolay Ugodnik (or Nikolay Chudotvorets, the Wonderworker) is Saint Nicholas, bishop of Myra (also known as Saint Nicholas of Bari), patron saint of travelers (sailors, merchants), prisoners, orphans and children in general, and others. Saint Nicholas is profoundly venerated by Russian Orthodoxy, and his life is often interpreted as concretizing various key ideas (wandering or continuous motion as source of salvation and purity; a mix of “otherness” and belonging). The figure of Saint Nicholas has served as the basis for a number of folkloric legends in Eastern Slavic tradition, and one of the most popular tales describes Nicholas as a wanderer across the Russian lands testing people for generosity, piety, and hospitality (see also T. Tsivian’s article “Nikolai Ugodnik — strannik na Russkoi zemle” 59).

text: Gury is one of the hunters living by the river. His death is described in detail in chapter 14: during an ice race, “a few verstas before the turn, Gury began gainin and the whipper-in fallin behind, but Gury aimed slightly more to the right than he should and fell into a polynya, an ice hole in the area of the fairway. [...] he plopped in and right away got sucked under the ice.” Since his body cannot be found until spring, his funeral is organized “without his factual presence” (R260/E196). This episode is already briefly alluded to in chapter 1: “He was the one that adored scrapin and rollin over the slick on his sharps, which additionally resulted in us losin a client, and the undertakers, in contrast, findin one” (R150/E3).

text: Orina, along with her variants, is the primary female character in the novel. In a sense, she is the only female figure in *Between Dog and Wolf*. As D.B. Johnson summarizes, the “promiscuous heroine Orina-Mariia is a train dispatcher, a princess in her dispatcher’s tower, who entertains her coworkers in her bed. Some of her orgiastic trysts take place near the train tracks to which her lovers tie her meddling husband Il'ia. Orina, in at least one time dimension, is killed by a train as she belatedly tries to save Il'ia who loses his leg” (“Twilight Cosmos” 647). Ilya is obsessed with this woman, and this passion “is the ultimate source of the woes that befall Il'ia, the itinerant grinder. It is his passion for the faithless slut Orina that brings about his misfortunes: the loss of his leg, his wandering life as a drunken grinder, and the grisly events that lead to his death” (643). Orina, alternatively called Maria, exists in the book also in another version, as *ta dama*, that dame, “a mysterious woman who appears along the river seeking Il'ia and, failing to find him, takes away a new lover each time [...]. Her chance lovers return days later, sexually depleted and without interest in life. They usually die by their own hand” (645). In this figure (which embodies “virtually all female figures in the book,” D.B. Johnson, “Sasha Sokolov’s *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 211), Sokolov merges two of his major literary themes: sex and death. Thus, Orina, Maria, that dame (*ta dama*, *ta devochka*, *ta bobylka*, *ta babulya* — all linked by the demonstrative “ta”), “Life Everlastin,” and death in general make up a unique polymorphic character. Smith notices that this female figure “does not appear at all in the verse. The episode of the sexual encounter between this figure and the sailors, which reoccurs obsessively in the prose, is correspondingly absent from the verse passages” (333). Olga Matich suggests the existence of a literary subtext for Sokolov’s novel: “Pilniak’s lesser known story *Mother Earth* (*Mat' syra zemlia* 1927) about the violent confrontation between a naive young Bolshevik and an archaic Volga peasant community at the time of the Civil War. It is a kind of love story between the city-bred Bolshevik and the horse-tanner and young earth mother Arina, impaled by the Cossacks in one of the story’s many violence-ridden episodes. A variation on the Scythian juxtaposition of nature and culture, the story also depicts Arina’s maternal love for a fox cub, whom she tries to tame, thinking it is a wolf” (“Sasha Sokolov and His Literary Context” 312). The name Orina may also carry an echo of Pushkin's famous nurse Arina Rodionovna (Toker 353). Mario Caramitti proposes three recurring hypostases of ta dama across Sokolov’s novels: a first hypostasis is that of a “mysterious woman carrying an obscure menace and/or sexual temptation”; a second hypostasis is that of an “apparently better defined and concrete woman being the object of desire for the main character”; and the third hypostasis is that of a “child-woman, often mentally retarded, often victim of violences, who touches upon a slightly more sublimated erotic sphere” (“Amore e morte” 114). Caramitti also adds that in the novel one of *ta dama*'s victims, before or after committing suicide, explicitly calls her “вечная жизнь” (Life Everlastin): “it is precisely in the coitus with eternity, in a region of oblivion that it is most difficult to place on this side or on the other side of the Lethe, that the male protagonist finds the widest surface of contact with this protean female entity of now vast symbolic implications” (118). Among Orina’s many lovers and among the men who take advantage of her, there is also Yakov, her son, who is in a way “re-enacting the role of the lame Oedipus” (Johnson, “Sasha Sokolov’s *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition” 212). In chapter 14, Orina’s patronymic is said to be “Ignat’evna” (daughter of Ignatii): the name Ignatii possibly comes from the Latin "ignis" (fire) (R258/E190). Given that Orina is depicted here through her lust, such a patronymic seems apt. Her last name is said to be alternatively Neklina and Paklina (Spacklin, in translation): “You were called around the barracks Orina Neklina, and to whom do you belong now, to what kind of, let’s suppose, Spacklin, ah?” (R246/E169). On the border with Ukraine, close to Mariupol' and to Chekhov’s hometown Taganrog, there is Rostov district named [Neklinovsky](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Neklinovsky+District,+Rostov+Oblast,+Russia/@47.3401775,38.4573479,10z/data=!3m1!4b1!4m6!3m5!1s0x40e15b225bc1e679:0xcfd2211cda636f94!8m2!3d47.4046214!4d38.9174539!16s%2Fm%2F0h3m72r?entry=ttu). *Paklia* and *paklina* are regional terms indicating different things: a left-handed person, an unhandy and clumsy person, a bony hand, a piece of hemp or coarse fiber, messy hair. The terms паклен and неклен are named for the Tatar maple (note the slight differences in the spelling between the tree names and Orina’s surnames: Неклина, Паклина). As Sokolov explains,  “Apparently, the author of the Notes and Ilya know or have heard about a man named Paklin. Ilya says that Arina's last name was Neklina, probably after one of her men. And now, years later, Ilya assumes, she lives with someone else, whose last name suggests to him the tree’s other name” (personal communication, July 7, 2023).
ru_trans: Орина (со всеми ее вариациями) является главным женским персонажем в романе. В каком-то смысле, она — единственная женская фигура в "Между собакой и волком". Как подытоживает Д. Б. Джонсон: “Героиня-гулена Орина-Мария — диспетчер поездов, принцесса в своей диспетчерской башне, развлекающая коллег в постели. Некоторые из ее оргиастических рандеву происходят рядом с железнодорожными путями, к которым любовники привязывают ее назойливого мужа Илью. Орина, по крайней мере, в одном из временных измерений, погибает под колесами поезда, тщетно пытаясь спасти потерявшего ногу Илью” (“Twilight Cosmos” 647). Илья одержим этой женщиной, и эта страсть “является первичным источником бед, постигающих странствующего точильщика Илью”. Именно его страсть к неверной Орине стала причиной его несчастий: потери ноги, бродячей жизни пьяного точильщика и страшных событий, приводящих к его смерти” (643). Орина, иначе называемая Марией, существует в романе и в иной вариации как та дама, “таинственная женщина, которая появляется у реки в поисках Ильи и, не найдя его, каждый раз уводит нового любовника [ …]. Ее случайные любовники возвращаются через несколько дней сексуально истощенные и лишенные интереса к жизни. Обычно они кончают жизнь самоубийством” (645). В этой фигуре, воплощающей в себе “практически все женские образы романа” (Johnson, “Sasha Sokolov’s 'Between Dog and Wolf' and the Modernist Tradition” 211), Соколов соединяет две свои основные литературные темы: секс и смерть. Таким образом, Орина, Мария, *та дама* (*та девочка, та бобылка, та бабуля* — все объединены указательным “та”), “вечная жизнь” и смерть в целом составляют уникальный полиморфный персонаж. Смит замечает, что эта женская фигура “ни разу не появляется в поэтических отрывках. Эпизод сексуального контакта между героиней и матросами, навязчиво повторяющийся в прозе, соответственно отсутствует в стихотворных главах” (333). О. Матич предполагает существование литературного подтекста романа Соколова: “Менее известный рассказ Пильняка 'Мать сыра-земля' (1927) о жестоком противостоянии наивного молодого большевика и архаичной волжской крестьянской общины в годы Гражданской войны. Это своего рода история любви воспитанного в городе большевика и кожевенницы, молодой матери-земли Арины, пронзенной казаками в одном из многочисленных кровопролитных эпизодов повести. Рассказ — вариация скифского сопоставления природы и культуры — изображает материнскую любовь Арины к лисенку, которого она пытается приручить, думая, что это волк” (“Sasha Sokolov and His Literary Context” 312). Имя Орина может также быть отголоском имени знаменитой пушкинской няни Арины Родионовны (Toker 353). М. Карамитти обозначает три повторяющиеся ипостаси “той дамы” в романах Соколова: первая ипостась — “таинственная женщина, несущая смутную угрозу и/или сексуальное искушение”; вторая ипостась — “явно более определенная и конкретная женщина, являющаяся объектом вожделения главного героя”; и третья ипостась — это “ребенок-девочка, часто умственно отсталая, часто жертва насилия, затрагивающая несколько более сублимированную эротическую сферу” (“Amore e morte” 114). Карамитти также добавляет, что в романе одна из жертв той дамы до или после своего самоубийства открыто называет ее “вечной жизнью”: “именно в соитии с вечностью, в области забвения, которую сложно поместить по ту или иную сторону Леты, главный герой достигает максимального контакта с этой многогранной женской сущностью, имеющей огромное символическое значение” (118). Среди многочисленных любовников Орины и пользующихся ею мужчин есть и ее сын Яков, который в каком-то смысле “воспроизводит роль хромого Эдипа” (Johnson, “Sasha Sokolov’s 'Between Dog and Wolf' and the Modernist Tradition” 212). В главе 14 упоминается отчество Орины — Игнатьевна (дочь Игнатия). Имя Игнатий вероятно происходит от латинского “ignis” (огонь) (Р258/Е190). Учитывая, как Орина изображается через свою похоть, такое отчество действительно уместно. Ее фамилия попеременно Неклина и Паклина (Спаклина в английском переводе): “Величали тебя по баракам — Орина Неклина, чья теперь ты, какого, положим, Паклина?” (Р246/Е169). Недалеко от украинской границы, около Мариуполя и Таганрога, родного города Чехова, в Ростовской области находится [Неклиновский район](https://www.google.com/maps/place/Neklinovsky+District,+Rostov+Oblast,+Russia/@47.3401775,38.4573479,10z/data=!3m1!4b1!4m6!3m5!1s0x40e15b225bc1e679:0xcfd2211cda636f94!8m2!3d47.4046214!4d38.9174539!16s%2Fm%2F0h3m72r?entry=ttu). "Пакля" и "паклина" — региональные термины, имеющие разнообразные значения: левша, неуклюжий и бездарный человек, костлявая рука, кусок пеньки или грубого волокна, растрепанные волосы. Термины паклен и неклен относятся к полевому клену (стоит обратить внимание на небольшие различия в написании названий дерева и фамилий Орины: Неклина, Паклина). Как поясняет Соколов: “Очевидно, автор Записок и Илья знают или слышали о человеке по фамилии Паклин. Илья говорит, что Орину звали Неклина, вероятно, по одному из ее мужей. А теперь, спустя годы, предполагает Илья, она живет с кем-то другим, фамилию которого подсказывает ему другое название дерева” (личная переписка, 7 июля 2023).Орина.

text: The main setting of the novel: a fictional town on the banks of the Volga River. Also called Gorodnishchi. Derived from the words for town (gorod) and beggar (nishchii). It is the "town of beggars." Olga Matich writes: "If *School for Fools* was written against the background of youth prose, Sokolov's next novel *Between Dog and Wolf* may be read as the author's response to village prose, the literary rage of the seventies" ("Sasha Sokolov" 310). Vadim Kreid observes that Gorodnishche, a barracks village of beggars and thieves, resembles an "Anti-Kitezh" (Kitezh being the legendary, mythical city in Russian folklore that only the pure-hearted will have the chance to reach). In Gorodnishche, however, thieves rob beggars, while beggars beg thieves ("Zaitil'shchina" 213). According to Johnson, the living dwell Gorodnishche, while the dead reside on the other side of the river, in Bydogoshch ("Sokolov's *Between Dog and Wolf* and the Modernist Tradition" 209). Johnson also mentions a statement by Sokolov himself: "Sokolov reports that the name is a blend of the dissolute eighteen-century town of Gorodnya described by A. N. Radishchev in his *Journey from Petersburg to Moscow* and a nearby town called Gorodishche. Thus the time layers of the sixteenth century, the eighteenth century, and a mythic present are all superimposed upon each other – a characteristic technique in the novel" (217).

text: Braid, scythe, or sandback/spit. The ambiguity of the word “kosa” has a famous literary “predecessor” in Aleksandr Blok’s drama *Balaganchik* (*The Puppet Show*, 1906). The female character of Columbine has a “kosa” behind her back: either a hair braid or a scythe. The “mystics” warn Pierrot about her being Death, but he calls her his bride (“Я не слушаю сказок. Я — простой человек. Вы не обманете меня. Это — Коломбина. Это — моя невеста”; I don't listen to fairy tales. I am a simple man. You will not deceive me. This is Columbine. This is my bride). The ambiguity is also stressed by the character of the Author who enters the scene and exclaims: “Я не признаю [...] аллегорической игры словами: неприлично называть косой смерти женскую косу! Это порочит дамское сословие!” (I do not recognize [...] such allegorical wordplay: it is indecent to call a woman's braid a scythe of death! It denigrates a lady's status!). In the end, Pierrot sadly discovers that this Columbine was just a “cardboard bride” (Она картонной невестой была). The crucial theme linking a woman’s love to death draws parallels between Sokolov’s novel and Blok’s *Balaganchik*, although there is a very long literary tradition that has developed this line (e.g., Eros and Thanatos; Catullus’s *Odi et amo*, *I hate and I love*). Read the original by Blok [here](https://ru.wikisource.org/wiki/%D0%91%D0%B0%D0%BB%D0%B0%D0%B3%D0%B0%D0%BD%D1%87%D0%B8%D0%BA_(%D0%91%D0%BB%D0%BE%D0%BA)).

text: Throughout the novel, geese are associated with sexual arousal. Here, they are linked to the Dama's appearance in the hunters' company. Although today far more commonly considered silly or stupid, geese have a lofty mythology. The goose has been traditional viewed as “an erotic symbol for both sexes, because it was the bird of creation, whether in the male solar form of the gods or the female lunar form of the mother goddesses" (Rowland, *Birds* 68). Similar connections between geese, sexuality, and foolishness appear elsewhere in the novel (R210, 221/E106, 125). Animal-human motif.
ru_trans: На протяжении романа, гуси ассоциируются с сексуальным возбуждением. Здесь, они связаны с появлением Дамы в компании охотников. Несмотря на современное восприятие гусей как глупых существ, мифологическая история этих птиц весьма благородна. Гуси традиционно воспринимались как "эротический символ обоих полов, будь то в форме солнца, олицетворяющего мужских богов, или луны, олицетворяющей богинь-матерей" (Rowland 68). Подобные связи между гусями, сексуальностью и глупостью встречаются далее в романе (R210, 221/E106, 125).
